Receptionist: Mr. Farmani's office. How can I help you?
Peter: Hello, could I speak to Farmani, please?
Receptionist: I'm afraid he's in a meeting until 2 p.m. Can I take a message?
Peter: Well, I'd like to arrange an appointment for Miranda to see him, please. It's Peter Smith here.

Receptionist: Can I put you on hold for a minute, Mr. Smith? I'll just look into the agenda. So when's convenient for you?
Peter: Is he available next Monday? Let's say around 2 p.m.?
Receptionist: I'm afraid he can't on Monday. What about Tuesday at 2 p.m.?
Peter: Ah, that could be awkward. Tuesday's appointments are rather scattered. Is there any possibility of meeting this Friday?
Receptionist: Well, Friday could work. We keep things rather flexible toward the end of the week. Could she meet at 2 p.m.?

Peter: Oh dear, she'll be in the middle of her status update meeting. Is there anything available toward the end of the day?
Receptionist: She has her plate full, doesn't she? Let me rearrange a few things ... Is 4 p.m. feasible?
Peter: Fantastic.

Receptionist: Alright. So shall we say Friday at 4 p.m. in your company's office?
Peter: Perfect. Thank you for your time.
Receptionist: You're welcome. Goodbye.
Setting Up an Appointment Over the Phone

In English, we have two different types of words:
a) grammatical or function words and
b) content words.

Content words are adjectives, adverbs, nouns and verbs. They are often stressed in spoken English. Grammatical words, on the other hand, are small words that basically help us build sentences and connect content words and do not carry any meaning. Articles, prepositions, conjunctions, auxiliary verbs, and determiners are all examples of grammatical words.

In spoken English, these words have no stress and are often weak. In other words, they are not pronounced as content words, which are strongly pronounced (“strong form”) and are often pronounced with a schwa sound. This is why they are difficult to hear when people are speaking.
In the following sentences, the weak forms are underlined.
Mr. Gibbs office. How can I help you?
Could I speak to Michael, please?
I'd like to arrange an appointment for Maria to see him.

Talking on the telephone can be challenging for a variety of reasons. Firstly, you are not able to see the person you're talking to, so there's no body language to be read. Secondly, it requires a special set of words, phrases, and expressions.
The chart below will help you to speak on the phone confidently in business and personal situations.

NOTE:
When talking about using the telephone, note the prepositions we use:

• on the phone (=talking using the telephone):
    I'm on the phone with Mr. Farmani.
    Most teenagers spend hours on the phone every day.

• by phone/over the phone (=using the telephone):
    We are doing business over the phone.
    We take orders by phone or by email.
not busy and has enough time to talk to you
Example: Is he available next week?

Example: That could be awkward. What about in the morning?
